# PowerRank

> PowerRank is an independent buying guide that ranks portable power stations and power banks by value: what you get for your money. Every model is scored with one published formula (capacity, outlets, power output and useful extras, compared against a typical selling price). No brand pays to be listed or ranked.

Site: https://powerrank.netlify.app/

## What the site does

- Visitors pick the devices they want to run or charge (for example a fridge, CPAP, laptop or phone) and how long they need power. PowerRank estimates the power and battery size needed, filters out models that can't handle it, and ranks the rest by value.
- Two categories: portable power stations (large batteries with wall outlets, rated in watt-hours) and power banks (pocket chargers, rated in mAh).
- Product specs come from manufacturer listings and are entered by hand. Specs and prices change, so confirm details on the product page before buying.
- Prices are not shown on the site. Each product links to Amazon for its current price ("Check price").

## How the value score works

- Capacity is weighted on a curve (capacity^0.585), so going from 500 Wh to 1,000 Wh counts for more than going from 2,000 Wh to 2,500 Wh.
- Each wall outlet, 240 V / high-amp outlet and USB port adds a fixed amount.
- Power output is scored against the power the visitor says they need; extra power beyond that adds nothing.
- Extras (expandable capacity, app support, jump-starting, MagSafe, built-in cables, a display, a built-in wall plug) each add a small fixed bonus.
- A typical selling price is subtracted. The value rating reflects where the result ranks within its category.
- It is one opinionated formula, not an objective truth; visitors can change the inputs with filters.

## Solar panels

- Only folding (portable) panels are listed. They're ranked by price per rated watt, lowest first. Weight and brand don't change the score.
- Pairing rule: aim for rated solar watts of about one third of the battery's watt-hours (roughly a full refill in one sunny day), never more than the station's solar input limit.
- A panel works with a station only if its open-circuit voltage (Voc), times the number of panels wired in series, stays inside the station's solar input voltage range.
- Real-world output in good sun is about 70-80% of a panel's rating.
- On the power stations page, an optional "Best value with solar" view ranks stations together with the cheapest matching solar setup.

## Quick sizing guide

- Charge phones and run a few lights or a fan for a night: about 300–500 Wh.
- Run a CPAP machine every night while camping: 500 Wh or more.
- Keep a fridge, lights and Wi-Fi going through a one-day outage: about 2,500–3,000 Wh.
- Get through a multi-day outage, or run bigger things like a space heater: 3,000 Wh or more.
- A 1,000 Wh battery runs a 100 W device for roughly 8–9 hours.
- A 10,000 mAh power bank charges a typical phone about twice; 20,000 mAh about four times.
- Power banks up to about 26,800 mAh (100 Wh) are generally allowed in carry-on bags, never in checked bags.
- LiFePO4 (LFP) batteries last thousands of charge cycles and are very safe.

## Disclosure

As an Amazon Associate, PowerRank earns from qualifying purchases. This does not affect rankings, which come only from the formula above.
